query/feature: Top-N of an OR of searches of one index: col @@> a OR col @@> b
condition: every branch is a match of the same index (at most 16), with no other predicate in the OR
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'a' OR body @@> 'b' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10
notes: The match set is the union of the branches. Without sift.score() each branch is bound as its own query: its errors and its phrase rechecks are the normal plan's. With sift.score() the OR is one ranked scan of the query a OR b: a row that matches two branches scores once, as that query does. A search ORed with a predicate on a column is S16.
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable' OR memo @@> 'wire' ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id LIMIT 10

query/feature: Top-N on a sift_table
example: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY a, id LIMIT 10
notes: The same top-N as on a sift_col index: the filters, the match set of a BM25 search and the numeric, date or integer sort columns are read from the column units and the write buffers, and the table only for the n rows of the result. A superblock is skipped when the zones of its units hold nothing better than the n-th row, whatever its place in the table: the new version of an updated row lands in the write buffer with any value. The limits of W09 to W12 apply.
query: SELECT id FROM cv_tt ORDER BY i4, id LIMIT 5

query/feature: Top-N rows of a partitioned table
example: SELECT id, total FROM orders_part ORDER BY total DESC, id LIMIT 5
notes: The partitions after pruning are one scan: each keeps its units, the heap holds the n best rows of all of them with the partition of each, and the winners are fetched from the partitions' heaps (the attribute numbers of a partition may differ). A text search of the table stays on the normal plan (S13).
query: SELECT id, total FROM orders_part ORDER BY total DESC, id LIMIT 5

query/feature: Plain SELECT ... WHERE of many rows, window functions over rows
condition: the column index serves aggregates and top-N, not row streams
example: SELECT id, total FROM t WHERE total > 400
notes: Use a btree index for row queries.
query: SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE total > 400

query/feature: Top-N by a text key under a nondeterministic collation, or by a char(n), name or cidr column
condition: not a name column of a sift_table
example: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY name COLLATE case_insensitive, id LIMIT 10
notes: Strings that a nondeterministic collation calls equal tie, and the next sort key orders them; a char(n) ignores its trailing spaces and a cidr orders its mask after its address, as the comparison function of each type does: the scan compares the entries of the unit's dictionary with that function under the collation of the call, so the rows are the normal plan's. A name column of a sift_table keeps the normal plan (the table stores it as a fixed-width value, not as a dictionary of strings); on a sift_col index it is a string key like the others.
query: -- guc: seq_page_cost = 10000\n-- guc: random_page_cost = 10000\nSELECT bool_and(coverage.same(q)) FROM unnest(ARRAY['SELECT id FROM orders ORDER BY status COLLATE coldiff_nd, id LIMIT 5', 'SELECT id FROM t_chars ORDER BY bp, id LIMIT 12 OFFSET 1', 'SELECT id FROM t_chars ORDER BY nm DESC NULLS FIRST, id LIMIT 12 OFFSET 1', 'SELECT id FROM cv_net ORDER BY cd, id LIMIT 12 OFFSET 1']) q

query/feature: Top-N by coalesce(int, date or timestamp column, constant), lower(text column), upper(text column)
example: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY coalesce(a, 0) DESC, id LIMIT 10
notes: These sort expressions cannot raise, so the scan that evaluates the key for every row that passes returns the normal plan's rows in its order. A NULL becomes the constant (the zone of a unit is widened to it, so units are skipped as for the column); lower() and upper() are PostgreSQL's own functions under the call's collation, called once per distinct entry of a unit. Any other expression is W10.
query: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY coalesce(customer_id, 500) DESC, id LIMIT 7

query/feature: Top-N page with the total of its set: aggregates over the whole set as window functions (count(*) OVER (), sum(x) OVER ())
example: SELECT id, total, count(*) OVER () FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' ORDER BY total, id LIMIT 5
notes: The scan keeps the heap of the n best and, in the same pass, computes the window aggregates from every row that passes (no unit is left out for the sort key's zone, and the scan is serial); every row of the page carries the totals. A window with PARTITION BY, ORDER BY or a frame that cuts the set, or a window function that is not an aggregate, keeps the normal plan (W15). An OFFSET past the last row returns no row, with or without the total.

query/feature: Top-N by an expression of the columns: arithmetic, casts, CASE, coalesce(a, b), NULLIF, GREATEST/LEAST, boolean tests, IN (..), lower(s || v), left(s, 3), md5(s), abs(a), round(n, 1), date_trunc('month', ts), a parameter of the statement
example: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY a + 1 DESC, id LIMIT 10
notes: The scan evaluates the expression with PostgreSQL's own expression machinery (the backend's operators, casts and comparison) for every row that passes the WHERE, as the plan's sort does, so overflow (integer out of range), division by zero, NULL and NaN behave as in the normal plan and an error has the same SQLSTATE (the message may name another row). Only immutable expressions over the integer, float, numeric (18 digits or fewer), date, time, timestamp, text and uuid leaves of the index; a volatile or stable one stays with the normal plan. Zones skip units only for a plain column; the other expressions read every unit that holds matching rows, so the cost model charges them per row and keeps the normal plan where it would be slower (numeric, casts to text). Any immutable function or operator of the builtin catalog or the user's (the types between the leaves and the key do not matter: only the leaves and the result are stored), with a string, number, date, time, bytea, uuid or inet result. A parameter of a generic plan is read from the leader's executor state, so the scan runs in the leader; a function that is not parallel safe does the same. CASE and coalesce keep their lazy order (a branch that is not taken does not raise), NULLs follow three-valued logic, strings compare under the collation of the column. The rest is W10.
query: SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY customer_id + 1 DESC, id LIMIT 7

query/feature: FOR UPDATE, TABLESAMPLE on the indexed heap table, a set-returning function in the select list of the aggregate
condition: row locks, sampling and per-row expansion are not aggregates over the index
example: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE
query: @trap/tablesample

query/feature: The first N rows of each group: row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY k ORDER BY o) cut by rn <= N (N > 1)
condition: the planner costs the grouped scan below the window; a small work_mem or a table without a gain keeps the window (sift.explain_why: window_first)
example: SELECT * FROM (SELECT grp, id, ts, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY grp ORDER BY ts, id) rn FROM events) s WHERE rn <= 3
notes: Planner only: the groups' arrays of each column, ordered, cut inside the group at N (up to 1,000) and unnested with their ordinal as rn; the scan keeps only the N best rows of each group as the rows pass (array_agg(x ORDER BY o)[1:N] in EXPLAIN). A nullable or several partition columns are the same form. rank() and dense_rank() <= N (up to 1,000) keep the rows that tie (the window function and its condition run above the rows the scan kept). N = 1 of row_number() is the DISTINCT ON rewrite. A table without a column index, a sub-select, an array or row typed column, or a window that is not this shape keeps the window.

query/feature: Parallel scan of the aggregate (count, sum, avg, min, max, count(DISTINCT), percentiles, keys of any kind, lookup joins, grouping sets)
example: SELECT tenant_id, count(*), sum(total) FROM orders GROUP BY tenant_id
notes: Workers are the ones a parallel sequential scan of the table would get (table size, parallel_workers, max_parallel_workers_per_gather) and are costed: a scan under about 15 ms keeps the leader alone. Not under a Gather: Workers Planned in the SiftAgg node. The merge of the workers' tables is costed per group: a query with hundreds of groups keeps the leader alone.

-- guc: parallel_setup_cost = 0
-- guc: parallel_tuple_cost = 0
-- guc: min_parallel_table_scan_size = 0
SELECT source, count(*), count(DISTINCT tenant_id) FROM cv_par GROUP BY source

query/feature: count(DISTINCT), sum(DISTINCT) and avg(DISTINCT) of numeric columns and numeric expressions (also dictionary and 32-bit integer values), percentiles, lookup-joined aggregates, per-order arms
example: SELECT source, count(DISTINCT total), sum(DISTINCT total) FROM orders GROUP BY source
notes: A worker sends the (group, value) pairs of its set, with the numbers themselves for a numeric value (the ids of its table of them are its own), and the leader gives them its own ids and counts or adds each once per group; a bitmap of 32-bit values goes as chunks that the leader ORs (X01). Proof: test `agg_distinct_parallel`.

query/feature: Float sums at any worker count
example: SELECT grp, sum(f8) FROM t GROUP BY grp
notes: 16 lanes added in lane order: the result is bit-identical for 0, 1, 2, ... workers and every SIMD level (not bit-identical to the heap-order sum of the normal plan).
query: SELECT coverage.workers_agree('SELECT tenant_id, sum(f), avg(f), count(*) FROM cv_par GROUP BY tenant_id')

query/feature: Generic aggregates with a combine function: stddev and variance, corr, regr_*, bit_and, bit_or, bit_xor, sum(float4)
engine: SELECT source, stddev(total), bit_or(tenant_id) FROM orders GROUP BY source
example: SELECT source, stddev(total), bool_and(total > 10) FROM orders GROUP BY source
notes: Each worker keeps the partial states per group and the leader merges them by key value with the aggregate's combine function. The ordered, DISTINCT and joined-column kinds stay serial (X06). bool_and and bool_or are the exception (X05).

-- guc: parallel_setup_cost = 0
-- guc: parallel_tuple_cost = 0

query/feature: bool_and, bool_or, every in a parallel plan
example: SELECT source, bool_and(tenant_id > 3) FROM orders GROUP BY source
notes: The partial states of the workers are merged by the aggregates' own combine functions.

-- guc: parallel_tuple_cost = 0

query/feature: DISTINCT in a generic aggregate (string_agg, array_agg), count(DISTINCT) of an expression or of a 64-bit leaf through a combination of values, sum(DISTINCT) of an integer, a lookup join on a value, ordered sets of generic aggregates
condition: run on the leader alone: no workers are planned (the reason is the aggregate: its partial state is not a set of numbers the leader can merge)
example: SELECT source, string_agg(DISTINCT status, ',') FROM orders GROUP BY source
notes: The scan is still the column scan; only the parallelism is missing.
query:
-- guc: max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 2
-- guc: parallel_setup_cost = 0
-- guc: parallel_tuple_cost = 0
-- guc: min_parallel_table_scan_size = 0
SELECT source, string_agg(DISTINCT status, ',') FROM orders GROUP BY source

query/feature: Shapes that need more than the sums of one key: up to four group keys, count(DISTINCT), sums of floats, and tests on a key of the cube or on a column the granule zones cover
example: SELECT source, status, count(*), count(DISTINCT tenant_id) FROM orders GROUP BY source, status
notes: A part of a format major 2 index keeps, in SEC_PREAGG version 2, a cube of all its rows, a cube for each of up to four keys of few values (dictionary text, integers, dates, bool) and one of the keys together: count, count of a column, sum, avg, min and max of up to eight integer, numeric or float columns, and the exact sets of distinct values of up to four columns (integers up to 64 a group, dictionary text of any size). A granule is answered from them when the query reads those columns, groups by keys of one cube and tests only those keys (equal, in, range, NULL, prefix) or columns whose zone says every row of the granule passes; any other granule is scanned in the same plan (`Answered By Pre-aggregate` and `Corrected For Dead Rows` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE). A float sum keeps the NaN and infinity of its rows, an integer sum has 128 bits. The serial scan and the workers of a parallel aggregate read them alike, and a cube over budget (4% of the granules) leaves out the granules that do not fit.

query/feature: Pre-aggregates serve the granules that churn left alone: after UPDATE or DELETE only the granules that changed are scanned, and VACUUM makes the rest exact again
condition: a granule is clean when every heap page of its rows is all-visible and no column delta or pending delete is in it; one with at most 64 dead rows (and under 5% of its rows) is corrected from its cube when the query reads counts and sums, or the minimum and maximum its dead rows do not hold; a count of distinct values and a float sum are scanned. A transaction sees its own changes by scanning the granules it changed. VACUUM writes the cubes of a rewritten part again
example: SELECT source, count(*), sum(total) FROM orders GROUP BY source
notes: The result never changes, only the speed: a granule that cannot be answered is scanned in the same plan and added to the exact ones; the granules of the same part that are clean still come from the cubes. Rows inserted later are parts of their own, answered once compaction writes their cubes.

query/feature: Pre-aggregates on a sift_table: a sealed part keeps cubes like a sift_col part, and granules with few dead rows are corrected from them
condition: a part is sealed by VACUUM (FREEZE) or maintenance (sift.table_maintain): rows still in the write buffer are scanned; a granule with more than 64 dead rows (or 5%) is scanned in the same plan
example: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(i4) FROM t GROUP BY grp
notes: The parts of a sift_table are written by the same writer as those of a sift_col index and carry the same cubes (SEC_PREAGG version 2), which the aggregate reads before it decodes a granule (`Answered By Pre-aggregate` and `Corrected For Dead Rows` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE). The answer is the heap's after INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and VACUUM; a table text column is lossy in the part, so the cubes of a table serve integer keys.

query/feature: GROUP BY one leaf of the elements of an array (jsonb_to_recordset, jsonb_array_elements, an array of strings): count(*), count(m), sum, avg, min and max of the integer and float8 leaves of the same array
condition: sift_col index of format minor 4 (3.1); a minor 3 segment has no element rollups
example: SELECT i.category, count(*), sum(i.qty), avg(i.price) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(o.items) AS i(category text, qty int, price float8) GROUP BY i.category
notes: Answered from the rollup of the elements of the exact units: the distinct tuples of the low-cardinality leaves of the array with their counts and the count, sum, min and max of its numeric leaves, written with the unit (the default takes the leaves of at most a 32nd of the unit's elements; `rollup = 'items[].category, items[].kind'` names the dims, AP11). A test on the grouped leaf (=, IN, IS NULL, LIKE) runs on the tuples, a comparison on a column of the rows is a zone test as for AP04. A unit whose array overflowed, or that has no rollup with the dims and measures the query reads, is scanned and asks for a refresh (AP12). Float sums add the tuples in another order than the rows: the last digits of a float8 sum may differ. A test on a leaf that is not a dim, count(DISTINCT) and an expression aggregate scan.
query: SELECT i.kind, count(*), sum(i.qty), avg(i.price) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(o.items) AS i(kind text, qty int, price float8) GROUP BY i.kind

query/feature: GROUP BY two or more leaves of the elements of an array, in any order or a subset of them, with tests on them (=, <>, IN, IS NULL, LIKE, OR): count, sum, avg, min, max of the numeric leaves
condition: sift_col index of format minor 4; units written with those leaves as dims (default: up to a 32nd of the elements as tuples, the dims of most distinct values dropped first; or the option rollup, AP11)
example: SELECT i.category, i.kind, count(*), sum(i.qty), min(i.price), max(i.price) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(o.items) AS i(category text, kind text, qty int, price float8) WHERE i.kind IN ('standard', 'gift') OR i.category = 'Toys' GROUP BY i.category, i.kind
notes: An aggregate with FILTER (WHERE ...) on dims is evaluated on the tuples (a tuple whose elements fail the filter adds nothing to that aggregate, and still makes its group). A group key that is a function of one dim (`upper(kind)`, `left(day, 7)`, a `CASE` or a division of an integer dim) is evaluated once per distinct value of the tuples, as for a column. Grouping sets (GROUPING SETS, ROLLUP, CUBE) over the dims fold the tuples once per set, the keys outside a set being NULL; GROUPING() keeps the scan. One rollup per unit and array answers every subset of its dims: the tuples that agree on the group key are added up, so there is no split order to choose and a query by one of the dims reads the same blob as one by all of them. A unit that lacks a dim of the query scans; the others answer in the same plan. count(DISTINCT), percentile_*, a test on a leaf that is not a dim and a high-cardinality key (more than 4096 tuples in a unit) are not covered by design (docs/COL-PREAGG.md section 1).
query: SELECT i.category, i.kind, count(*), sum(i.qty), min(i.price), max(i.price) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(o.items) AS i(category text, kind text, qty int, price float8) WHERE i.kind IN ('standard', 'gift') OR i.category = 'Toys' GROUP BY i.category, i.kind

query/feature: GROUP BY the key of a map (jsonb_each, jsonb_each_text): count, sum, avg, min, max of the value, tests on the key
condition: sift_col index of format minor 4; the map declared as m.* in paths
example: SELECT m.key, count(*), sum(m.value::float8), avg(m.value::float8), min(m.value::float8), max(m.value::float8) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_each_text(o.metrics) m WHERE m.key IN ('m_total', 'packaging') OR m.key LIKE 'check%' GROUP BY m.key
notes: The key of the map is the dim of the rollup of the map and its value the measure; the key ids of the unit are translated to the keys of the query as for a column. A test on the value, and a value cast other than to the declared type, scan. Format 2.0 keeps a cube of the members of each map whose keys the part holds as a dictionary: for each key of a granule the count, the sum, the least and the greatest of its values. A granule whose rows the snapshot sees whole is answered from it (`preagg=N` of EXPLAIN ANALYZE), the key tests run on the keys of its cells; a granule with a dead row, a heap page that is not all-visible, or a value or a document the leaves cannot hold is read from its columns (`Unnest Value`), with the key tests run on the keys first.
query: SELECT m.key, count(*), sum(m.value::float8), avg(m.value::float8), min(m.value::float8), max(m.value::float8) FROM orders o CROSS JOIN LATERAL jsonb_each_text(o.metrics) m WHERE m.key IN ('m_total', 'packaging') OR m.key LIKE 'check%' GROUP BY m.key

query/feature: CREATE INDEX or ALTER INDEX with a rollup option that names a leaf that is not a low-cardinality leaf of an array element or a map value declared in paths (or names it twice, or more than 6 for a list)
condition: 22023 at CREATE INDEX and ALTER INDEX; name integer, date, numeric, boolean or text leaves of an array of objects or a map declared in paths, or drop the option (rollup = 'off' disables the rollups)
example: CREATE INDEX orders_roll_bad ON orders USING sift_col (id, items) WITH (paths = 'items[]{category text, qty int4}', rollup = 'items[].nosuch')
notes: WITH (rollup = 'items[].kind, items[].sub') names the dims of the rollups of the lists (the measures are their numeric leaves); the units written afterwards hold exactly these dims, up to 4096 tuples each and no byte budget, and the units written before are asked for on demand (AP12) or rewritten by a merge. The error names the leaf; a leaf with too many distinct values is not an error of the DDL: the unit holds no rollup for that list and scans.
query: CREATE INDEX orders_roll_bad ON orders USING sift_col (id, items) WITH (paths = 'items[]{category text, qty int4}', rollup = 'items[].nosuch')

query/feature: After ALTER INDEX changes preagg, rollup or cube_minmax, the segments written before keep the old sections; sift.col_refresh(index) rewrites the ones that differ from what the options ask now, one segment at a time, with the same answers
condition: sift.col_refresh(index, max_segments); a segment of a minor above sift.col_format_minor is left as written; not on a hot standby
example: SELECT * FROM sift.col_refresh('orders_col', 0)
notes: Each segment is the atomic replacement of a merge of it alone, under the maintenance lock that readers and writers do not wait for; a cancel or a crash leaves the segments done and the one in hand as it was, and the call made again goes on. max_segments bounds the rewrites of a call (NULL: all, 0: only count what is stale). The planner counts the units that hold the histogram of a dim, its min and max, or the rollup of a list, and prices a scan answered from them by that share, so a half refreshed index costs between the two. Space freed is reused after VACUUM.
query: SELECT count(*) = 1 FROM pg_proc WHERE proname = 'col_refresh' AND pronamespace = 'sift'::regnamespace

query/feature: Calendar cells of a date or timestamp beside jsonb paths: GROUP BY date_trunc(month, d) and date ranges of an index with paths
example: CREATE INDEX ON t USING sift_col (id, d, doc) WITH (paths = 'doc.a int4', calendar_columns = 'all'); SELECT date_trunc('month', d), count(*) FROM t GROUP BY 1
notes: Opt-in with paths (3.4: calendar_columns = all or a list; 3.3 refused the combination): +9.3% to +12.1% of an index with three date columns. A range with day bounds cuts the month cells at its ends and answers the cells inside from the pre-aggregates; a date without a histogram is tested by its cells.

query/feature: A filter col IS NULL on a column that is NULL in nearly every row (a soft-delete stamp): the granules are answered from the cubes, whose NULL group is the rows the filter keeps
condition: at most 2% of the rows of the part have a value in the column; a granule with more than 512 groups of the cube, or with dead rows over the cap, is scanned in the same plan
example: SELECT kind, count(*), sum(val) FROM t WHERE stamp IS NULL GROUP BY kind
notes: A column of which at most 2% of the rows have a value is a dimension of the cubes of the part whatever its values: the rows of a granule that have one make a few cells of their own beside the NULL group of each key, so `stamp IS NULL`, `stamp IS NOT NULL` and a group by the stamp are answered from the cells of the granule (`Answered By Pre-aggregate` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE) and the rows that keep a stamp are not read. Before it, a stamp with a value of its own in each row of a few made the column too wide to be a dimension and every granule a scan.

query/feature: Rows inserted after the index was built, not yet vacuumed (pages not all-visible)
example: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v) FROM t GROUP BY grp
notes: Rows on pages the visibility map does not cover are checked in the heap under the query's snapshot, after the value filters.
query: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v), avg(f) FROM cv_dml GROUP BY grp

query/feature: Updated and deleted rows, rolled-back inserts (dead versions before VACUUM)
example: SELECT tx, count(*) FROM t GROUP BY tx
notes: An UPDATE of an indexed column is a new tuple with its own index record.
query: SELECT tx, count(*), min(v), max(v) FROM cv_dml WHERE id % 25 <> 1 GROUP BY tx

query/feature: The transaction's own uncommitted changes
example: BEGIN; INSERT ...; SELECT count(*) ...;
notes: Compared with the normal plan in every state.
query: SELECT coverage.in_tx(ARRAY['INSERT INTO cv_dml SELECT 20000 + i, i % 5, i, i, ''n'' FROM generate_series(1, 100) i', 'UPDATE cv_dml SET v = v + 1 WHERE id % 7 = 0', 'DELETE FROM cv_dml WHERE id % 11 = 0'], 'SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v), min(v) FROM cv_dml GROUP BY grp') AND coverage.in_tx(ARRAY['INSERT INTO cv_tt SELECT * FROM cv_types WHERE id <= 40', 'UPDATE cv_tt SET i4 = i4 + 1 WHERE id % 9 = 0', 'DELETE FROM cv_tt WHERE id % 13 = 0'], 'SELECT grp, count(*), sum(i4) FROM cv_tt GROUP BY grp')

query/feature: Long snapshots, uncommitted writers, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE
example: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; SELECT ...
notes: A SERIALIZABLE scan takes a relation predicate lock, so concurrent writers can cause 40001: retry.
query: SELECT coverage.snapshot('repeatable read', 'SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v) FROM cv_snap GROUP BY grp', ARRAY['INSERT INTO cv_snap SELECT 5000 + i, i % 5, i FROM generate_series(1, 200) i', 'UPDATE cv_snap SET v = v + 1 WHERE id % 7 = 0', 'DELETE FROM cv_snap WHERE id % 13 = 0']) AND coverage.snapshot('serializable', 'SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v) FROM cv_snap GROUP BY grp', ARRAY['INSERT INTO cv_snap SELECT 5000 + i, i % 5, i FROM generate_series(1, 200) i', 'UPDATE cv_snap SET v = v + 1 WHERE id % 7 = 0', 'DELETE FROM cv_snap WHERE id % 13 = 0'])

query/feature: VACUUM, REINDEX, promotion and merge of the segments, TID reuse
example: VACUUM orders; SELECT ...

query/feature: HOT updates of columns no index holds
example: UPDATE orders SET total = total + 1
query: -- pre: UPDATE cv_hot SET pad = pad || 'x' WHERE id % 2 = 0;\nSELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM heap_page_items(get_raw_page('cv_hot', 0)) WHERE (t_infomask2 & 16384) <> 0) AND coverage.same('SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v), max(id) FROM cv_hot GROUP BY grp')

query/feature: Hot standby (physical replica)
example: SELECT ... on the standby
notes: The index is generic WAL: a standby serves the scans read-only. A logical subscriber builds its own index (proof: script:replication).
query: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(v) FROM cv_dml GROUP BY grp

query/feature: All terms: body @@> 'cable wire' (words are ANDed)
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'battery friendly'
notes: Case and accent folded; optional Snowball English stemming (stemmer = 'en').
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable wire'

query/feature: OR, parentheses, set of words {a b c}, boost ^n
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> '(case OR clip) AND friendly^3'
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> '((cable OR wire) AND gift^3) OR {box label}'

query/feature: NOT (exclusion)
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'battery NOT squeaky'
notes: A NOT needs a positive term in its AND group.
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable NOT wire'

query/feature: Phrase: "friendly staff"
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> '"friendly staff"'
notes: Decided from the word positions in the index (positions = on, the default); with positions = off, rechecked in the heap.
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> '"gift invoice"'

query/feature: Prefix (cle*), wildcard (w?fi), regex (/thank.*/), fuzzy (clen~1)
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'brea* OR n?isy OR /no.*y/ OR frendly~1'
notes: Above sift.max_expansions (512) terms a leaf scores as one term. A regex has no back-references.
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cle* OR w?fi OR /thank.*/ OR clen~1'

query/feature: Field weights: sift.field_query(query, 'title^3, body') over the sections of one key; name:word, name:(a b), name:{a b}
condition: the index is built with the fields option on a key made by sift.sections(...)
example: sift.sections(title, body) @@> sift.field_query('wireless', 'title^3, body')
notes: Weights are set per query and a row scores the sum of its fields. BM25F: a leaf of a field is scored with the length of that field in the row and its average over the rows ([FORMAT.md](FORMAT.md)); no analyzer per field, regular expressions are not scoped to a field; name:"a b" is a phrase of that section, and no phrase holds across the boundary of two sections ([SEARCH.md](SEARCH.md)). Without fields a colon is plain text. prefix_index = n makes short prefixes one lookup (autocomplete).
query: SELECT id FROM cv_places WHERE (name || chr(29) || admin1 || ' ' || country) @@> '(gr* ho*) AND (name:{gr* ho*}^3 OR (gr* ho*))' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 20

query/feature: Ranked top-k: ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT k
example: SELECT id, sift.score(ctid) FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'case OR clip' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 10
notes: Exact BM25; skips blocks that cannot reach the top k; ties break by ctid. Also with a prepared LIMIT $1 and on materialized views.
query: SELECT id, sift.score(ctid) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable OR wire' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 10

query/feature: count(*) of a match
example: SELECT count(*) FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'friendly'
notes: Counted from the index (SiftCount). With another filter in the WHERE, a SiftScan feeds PostgreSQL's count.
query: SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable wire'

query/feature: Match with other filters: score ranking plus a range or equality filter
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'friendly' AND published >= '2026-02-01' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 10
notes: With sift.filter_pushdown (on) the bitmap of the other quals (btree, BRIN, GIN) goes into the ranked scan, so a selective filter stays fast; results equal the post-filter plan. Prepared statements keep the filter as a child built only when it pays.
query: SELECT id, sift.score(ctid) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable OR wire' AND placed_at >= DATE '2025-01-01' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 10

query/feature: Join with ranking
example: SELECT d.id, c.name FROM docs d JOIN categories c ON c.id = d.category WHERE d.body @@> 'friendly' ORDER BY sift.score(d.ctid) DESC LIMIT 10
notes: Nested loop; semi joins too.
query: SELECT o.id, s.kind FROM orders o JOIN tenants s ON s.id = o.tenant_id WHERE o.memo @@> 'damaged' ORDER BY sift.score(o.ctid) DESC LIMIT 10

query/feature: Several queries ORed: body @@> ANY (ARRAY['case', 'clip'])
condition: scored like the OR in one query text; an unscored list above 100,000 rows stays a bitmap scan
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> ANY (ARRAY['case', 'clip'])
notes: Same matches, scores and ranking as `a OR b`; count, LIMIT and top-N use the scan. Medians of 9 runs: count(*) 1.6-54x faster, LIMIT 1.5-130x faster (0.1 ms slower when the whole query takes under 0.2 ms), full list equal or up to 2x faster, plan under 0.6 ms at 100 elements.
query: SELECT id, sift.score(ctid) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> ANY (ARRAY['cable', 'wire']) ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 3

query/feature: Keyword facets: sift.facets(index, facet_index, query, limit)
condition: keyword analyzer, text keys
example: SELECT * FROM sift.facets('docs_body', 'docs_category', 'friendly OR case', 10)
notes: Counts per value from the bitmaps, equal to the GROUP BY of the same snapshot; a row the row-level security policies of the caller hide counts in no value (a table with policies is read as the caller's own SELECT reads it); wins on broad queries over low-cardinality columns, GROUP BY wins on selective ones or thousands of values.
query: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT value::text, count::bigint FROM sift.facets('orders_fts', 'orders_src_kw', 'cable OR wire', 100) EXCEPT ALL SELECT source, count(*) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable OR wire' GROUP BY source) x

query/feature: Partitioned tables: matching, count(*) and ranking through the parent
example: SELECT id FROM logs WHERE msg @@> 'disk "node 7"' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 3
notes: One index per leaf partition, global top-k by a MergeAppend. Scores are per partition statistics; sift.score() needs an index on every partition read.
query: SELECT id, sift.score(ctid) FROM cv_logs WHERE msg @@> 'disk "node 7"' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 3

query/feature: Several columns in one index
condition: build one key with sift.sections(a, b) (or concatenate the columns) and query with the same expression
example: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING sift (sift.sections(title, body)) WITH (fields = 'title,body')
notes: A multicolumn index is refused (next rows).
query: SELECT id FROM cv_places WHERE (name || chr(29) || admin1 || ' ' || country) @@> 'gr*' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 5

query/feature: Match on a column with no sift index
condition: no index: the operator runs per row, with the same results
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE title @@> 'noisy'
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE country_code @@> 'US'

query/feature: A match ORed with a predicate on another column
condition: two branches, a constant query and quals the store decides (a sift_col index of the table or a sift_table), none reading a score; no index on the other column
example: WHERE body @@> 'a' OR category = 1
notes: The rows the quals take come from one scan of the store, then the matches they do not take, so a heap or a sift_table needs no index on the other column; EXPLAIN shows Hybrid Direction: OR. An aggregate over it is one SiftHybridAgg: the rows the quals take are folded from the store into a tid set, then the matches outside it from the heap, with no tuple handed to an aggregate above. With sift.score() or an order by it the normal plan stays.

query/feature: BM25 index on a sift_table
example: SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE tx @@> 'tx7'
notes: ambuild and scans run through the table access method.
query: SELECT count(*) FROM cv_tt WHERE tx @@> 'tx7'

query/feature: Parallel scan of a match (Gather over SiftScan / SiftCount)
condition: sift.parallel_scan = on (off by default); a ranked scan needs a LIMIT and one table; a ranked scan over partitions is a Merge Append of their scans, which share the k-th best score of the searches before them (EXPLAIN: Shared Floor)
example: SET sift.parallel_scan = on
notes: A Gather costs milliseconds: it paid only for heavy residual quals on 218,058 articles (1.8x). A pushed-down filter is built by every participant from the same snapshot; an unordered scan or count over partitions runs under a Parallel Append.
query:
-- pre: ALTER TABLE orders SET (parallel_workers = 2);
-- guc: sift.parallel_scan = on
-- guc: max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 2
-- guc: parallel_setup_cost = 0
-- guc: parallel_tuple_cost = 0
-- guc: min_parallel_table_scan_size = 0
-- guc: min_parallel_index_scan_size = 0
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'damaged' AND length(memo) > 3

query/feature: Hot standby, replication, VACUUM, REINDEX CONCURRENTLY, pg_dump
notes: MVCC, generic WAL, partial and expression indexes. Logical replication carries rows, not indexes: create the index on the subscriber.
query: -- pre: VACUUM orders;\n-- pre: REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_fts;\nSELECT pg_get_indexdef('orders_fts'::regclass) LIKE '%USING sift (memo)%' AND coverage.plan_of('SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> ''clean''') ~ 'Custom Scan \(Sift(Scan|Count)\)'

query/feature: Facets: sift.facet_counts(table, key, query, facets): terms with top N, range, histogram, date and array facets, several per call, multi-select
example: SELECT * FROM sift.facet_counts('orders', 'memo', 'cable OR wire', '[{"expr":"source","size":5},{"expr":"total","edges":[100,300]}]')
notes: Exact counts of the same snapshot; each facet is its own scan, a Custom Scan (SiftAgg) when the columns are in the sift_col index, the normal plan (same counts) for an array facet or a column outside it. See [SEARCH.md](SEARCH.md).
query: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT value, count FROM sift.facet_counts('orders', 'memo', 'cable OR wire', '["source"]') WHERE kind = 'value' EXCEPT ALL SELECT source, count(*) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable OR wire' GROUP BY source) x

query/feature: Aggregate over the rows of a match: GROUP BY with @@> in the WHERE
condition: the table has a sift_col index with the grouped and aggregated columns, or is a sift_table whose store holds them (integer, boolean, date and time columns); the planner takes the match set when its cost is lower, else SiftScan and a normal aggregate
example: SELECT source, count(*) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable' GROUP BY source
notes: The BM25 index gives the match set without reading the heap, the column store aggregates the matching rows (filters, generic aggregates, HAVING, parallel workers as for any SiftAgg); EXPLAIN shows Search: <index> @@> <query>. For counts per value of a keyword column, sift.facets also works.
query: SELECT source, count(*) AS n, count(DISTINCT tenant_id) AS stores, min(placed_at) FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'cable wire' AND deleted_at IS NULL GROUP BY source ORDER BY source

query/feature: Aggregate over a ranked top-k (subquery with LIMIT) or a column aggregate joined to a ranked scan
example: SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'damaged' ORDER BY sift.score(ctid) DESC LIMIT 100) GROUP BY 1
notes: The ranked scan stays on SiftScan, as the plan under the node: its rows are read once when the aggregate starts and become a table of keys (a byte table for an integer or date key). The aggregate joined to the ranked scan with its score is the same join. The top-k must fit half of work_mem.
query: @subplan/topk_in

query/feature: sift.score() compared with a constant in WHERE (> >= < <=, either side): a minimum or maximum score
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'a' AND sift.score(ctid) > 1
notes: The scan tests the cutoff on the score it computed, so the rows are those of a subquery that filters on the score; the score does not depend on the cutoff. A cutoff from below keeps the LIMIT hint of the ranked scan, one from above reads every match. A constant, a parameter or a stable expression of them; several cutoffs must all hold. BETWEEN and NOT (score > c) are such comparisons once PostgreSQL has rewritten them; OR, =, <>, an expression of the score, max_score() and a score of another query level stay 0A000: filter on the score from a subquery.
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'damaged' AND sift.score(ctid) > 1

query/feature: sift.score() in UPDATE, DELETE and FOR UPDATE
example: UPDATE t SET ... WHERE sift.score(ctid) > 0
notes: RETURNING sift.score(ctid) of an UPDATE or DELETE gives the score of the row the statement matched.
query: UPDATE orders SET status = status WHERE sift.score(ctid) > 0 AND memo @@> 'damaged'

query/feature: NOT with no positive term: body @@> 'NOT wire'
example: SELECT id FROM docs WHERE body @@> 'NOT noisy'
notes: Answers the rows that do not have the term. Also: queries over 256 leaves, nesting depth 32, phrases over 128 tokens, boosts over 10000 are refused (42601).
query: SELECT id FROM orders WHERE memo @@> 'NOT wire'

query/feature: BM25 index on several columns, a unique index, INCLUDE columns, a non-text key
example: CREATE INDEX ON docs USING sift (title, body)
notes: A unique index refuses a duplicate key at insert. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT arbitrates on a UNIQUE index (DO NOTHING and DO UPDATE).
query: DO $$ BEGIN CREATE INDEX cv_x ON orders USING sift (memo, status); DROP INDEX cv_x; END $$

query/feature: sift_col: unique, INCLUDE
condition: format major 2 (the default); the key of a UNIQUE index is an integer, boolean, date, timestamp, numeric, uuid, text or varchar column; INSERT ... ON CONFLICT needs PostgreSQL 18 (17 refuses a table with a unique index that is not a btree) and works with the default operator class of the type (a numeric key names sift.col_numeric_ops)
example: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON t USING sift_col (id) INCLUDE (payload)
notes: INCLUDE columns are stored like key columns and returned by index-only scans (return_columns). A unique index refuses a second live row of a key at the build and at each write (23505), waits for the transaction that wrote or deleted the key (the keys of the rows a transaction has not flushed are in a registry in shared memory, so a unique insert does not flush its row), and keeps NULLs distinct unless NULLS NOT DISTINCT. An index of format major 1, a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint (PostgreSQL asks a btree for a constraint) and a key of another type are refused.

query/feature: Aggregates over a sift_table: count, sum, avg, min, max, distinct, filters, grouping
example: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(i4) FROM t WHERE i4 > 100 GROUP BY grp
notes: The same SiftAgg node reads the column groups, the write buffer (as in-memory batches) and the tombstones with the table's own visibility; no index is needed.
query: SELECT grp, count(*), sum(i4), min(d) FROM cv_tt WHERE i4 > 100 GROUP BY grp

query/feature: Backward scan: a SCROLL cursor fetching backward, FETCH PRIOR / LAST
example: DECLARE c SCROLL CURSOR FOR SELECT * FROM t; FETCH LAST FROM c; FETCH PRIOR FROM c
notes: Both directions, as a heap: the first backward step lists the units of the range and walks them from the last; no unit is decoded twice per step.
query: SELECT coverage.scroll_back('cv_tt')

query/feature: More than 1,600 columns (127 on a table of format major 1)
condition: 54011 at CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE, PostgreSQL's own limit; a table of format major 1 refuses more than 127 columns with 54000
example: CREATE TABLE t (c1 int, ..., c1601 int) USING sift_table
notes: ADD COLUMN past the limit fails as CREATE TABLE does; DROP COLUMN is not checked. Format major 2 keeps every column PostgreSQL allows (1,600).
query: DO $d$ BEGIN EXECUTE 'CREATE TEMP TABLE cv_w1601 (' || (SELECT string_agg('c' || g || ' int', ',') FROM generate_series(1, 1601) g) || ') USING sift_table'; END $d$

query/feature: TID range scans (ctid >= ... AND ctid < ...)
example: SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE ctid >= '(0,1)' AND ctid < '(100,1)'
notes: A plain row scan: the aggregate scan does not take a ctid qual.
query: SELECT count(*) FROM cv_tt WHERE ctid >= '(0,1)' AND ctid < '(100,1)'

query/feature: TABLESAMPLE SYSTEM and BERNOULLI
example: SELECT count(*) FROM t TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (10) REPEATABLE (7)
notes: A heap table with a column index keeps the normal plan for TABLESAMPLE (No in the aggregate rows).
query: SELECT count(*) > 0 FROM cv_tt TABLESAMPLE BERNOULLI (50)

query/feature: COPY in and out, INSERT ... SELECT, CREATE TABLE AS, ALTER TABLE ... SET ACCESS METHOD
example: COPY t FROM STDIN
notes: Rows go through the write buffer one at a time (no bulk column path).

query/feature: Row scans of some columns (SELECT a FROM t WHERE ...), btree, GIN, BRIN, BM25 indexes, bitmap scans
example: SELECT i4 FROM t WHERE i4 < 10
notes: Works as for a heap; a table access method is not told which columns a query needs, so every row scan decodes whole units. Only the aggregate scan reads just its columns.
query: SELECT i4 FROM cv_tt WHERE i4 < 10

query/feature: UPDATE, DELETE, ON CONFLICT, row locks, triggers, savepoints, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER
condition: no HOT; an UPDATE of a quarter of the columns of a table of four or more that no index holds, with no row trigger or transition table on the update, changes the column in place; FOR KEY SHARE never conflicts with a non-key UPDATE
example: UPDATE t SET ... WHERE ...
notes: An UPDATE writes a new version and a tombstone, both visible to the aggregate scan under MVCC, or changes the column in place (same TID). A shared row lock stays shared when it is escalated: FOR KEY SHARE and FOR SHARE do not block a non-key UPDATE of the row.

query/feature: System columns xmin, xmax, cmin, cmax
example: SELECT xmin FROM t
notes: ctid, tableoid, xmin, xmax, cmin and cmax are the row's: xmin and cmin the stored versions of its insertion (FrozenTransactionId once frozen), xmax and cmax those of its last delete or update (0 if none); a table of format major 1 shows its last lock too, a table of format major 2 none.

query/feature: Publishing a sift_table under wal_level = logical without pg_sift in shared_preload_libraries
condition: 0A000 at CREATE or ALTER PUBLICATION (the event trigger sift_publication_check); preload pg_sift on the publisher and its standbys, or publish a heap staging table
example: CREATE PUBLICATION p FOR TABLE t
notes: A subscriber needs nothing. Unpublished tables never need the preload.
query: CREATE PUBLICATION cv_p FOR TABLE cv_pub

query/feature: An inner join that returns a column of the table, or a semi join, on an integer (int8 too) or date leaf: the keys of the loaded table are tested against the leaf before tuples are made
example: SELECT s.kind, count(*) FROM orders o JOIN tenants s ON s.id = o.tenant_id WHERE s.country_code = 'DE' GROUP BY s.kind
notes: The keys of the rows the table holds (its own conditions applied while loading) are a byte table over their range (a hash table when they span more than 4 million values), a conjunct of the scan: units the range misses are not read, the other rows are tested as a set before the combo cache is asked (sift.agg_join_filter, Join Key Filters of EXPLAIN ANALYZE). LEFT, RIGHT, FULL and anti joins and text keys keep the generic join, with the same rows.
query: @join/filter_inner

query/feature: UNION ALL arms (or an inlined CTE read several times) that join the same table with the same columns and conditions
example: SELECT 'a', s.kind, count(*) FROM orders o JOIN tenants s ON s.id = o.tenant_id WHERE s.country_code = 'US' GROUP BY s.kind UNION ALL SELECT 'b', s.kind, count(*) FROM orders o JOIN tenants s ON s.id = o.tenant_id WHERE s.country_code = 'US' AND o.deleted_at IS NULL GROUP BY s.kind
notes: The first arm loads the table into a context of the statement and the other arms use its rows (sift.agg_share_lookups, Shared Lookup Tables of EXPLAIN ANALYZE); arms that read other columns or conditions of the table, plans as tables and preserved sides load their own. A backend keeps the rows of a vacuumed, unchanged table for its next statement (sift.agg_lookup_cache_kb, Cached Lookup Tables).
query: @join/share_arms

query/feature: An EXISTS over the elements of an array leaf, written with a sub-select that PostgreSQL pulls up
example: SELECT w.dim_a_id % 5, count(*) FROM t_work w WHERE EXISTS (SELECT * FROM LATERAL (SELECT sign, score FROM jsonb_to_recordset(doc_norm(w.doc) -> 'parts') AS o(category text, sign text, score float8) WHERE o.score IS NOT NULL) o WHERE o.sign = 'positive') GROUP BY 1
notes: The sub-select is pulled up by PostgreSQL into the EXISTS: the sub-plan has the function, its conditions and the dead entry of the sub-select; the scan tests the elements as for the plain form.
query: @nested/exists_pulled_up

query/feature: Conditions of the nullable input of an outer join that test the arrays of its rows (an EXISTS, a jsonpath test), and the aggregate filters that read a test computed inside it
condition: a computed test that is true for an absent input (`x IS NULL`) keeps the normal plan
example: SELECT s.kind, count(DISTINCT w.id) FILTER (WHERE w.managed IS TRUE) FROM tenants s LEFT JOIN (SELECT x.id, x.dim_a_id, jsonb_path_exists(x.comments, '$[*] ? (@.type == "type_a")') AS managed FROM t_work x WHERE x.deleted_at IS NULL) w ON w.dim_a_id = s.id WHERE s.id <= 40 GROUP BY 1
notes: The ON conjuncts that read only the scanned table filter its rows before matching, like the conditions of a sub-select pulled up, and a placeholder computed inside the input is read through its guard (`CASE WHEN absent THEN NULL ELSE x END`) when the test is not true for an absent input.
query: @nested/left_derived

query/feature: A WITH inside a derived table (a ranked top-N over an aggregate, UNION ALL arms that read one CTE of it)
condition: the derived table reads nothing of the queries around it (a lateral one that does keeps the normal plan)
example: SELECT r.kind, r.n FROM (SELECT t.*, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY t.n DESC, t.kind) AS rn FROM (WITH scope AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT DISTINCT id FROM tenants WHERE country_code <> 'ZZ') SELECT s.kind, count(*) AS n FROM orders o JOIN scope c ON c.id = o.tenant_id JOIN tenants s ON s.id = c.id WHERE o.deleted_at IS NULL GROUP BY s.kind) t) r WHERE r.rn <= 3
notes: The CTEs of such a derived table are lookup plans of the scan like the statement's own, and a CTE of it that several aggregates read is planned inline when the arms run on the index (the plan that costs less wins).
query: @nested/cte_lookups

query/feature: A join to a sub-select whose rows the plan of the sub-select already filters (the run condition of a ranking window, a top-N per group)
example: SELECT s.kind, count(*) FROM orders o JOIN tenants s ON s.id = o.tenant_id WHERE o.tenant_id IN (SELECT tenant_id FROM (SELECT tenant_id, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY kind ORDER BY n DESC, tenant_id) AS rn FROM (SELECT o2.tenant_id, s2.kind, count(*) AS n FROM orders o2 JOIN tenants s2 ON s2.id = o2.tenant_id GROUP BY 1, 2) c) ranked WHERE rn <= 3) GROUP BY 1
notes: A condition over the columns of a joined sub-select that PostgreSQL pushed down into it is enforced by its plan, which then does not output the column: the scan does not test it again (a column the query reads stays in the output, and the condition is tested as usual).
query: @nested/pushed_rank_semi

query/feature: EXISTS over the elements of an array whose test reads a lookup per element (a mapping table by the element and a column of a joined table) or a column of a joined table
condition: the sub-select reads the array of the row, a lookup LIMIT 1 on columns of the element and the joined table, and nothing that can raise; EXISTS in the WHERE (also under an outer join); no workers
example: @ee_mapped_category
notes: Each element is looked up once per distinct value of the columns the lookup reads (PostgreSQL's plan of the lookup, run on the first need); a row passes when some element does, as in the normal plan, and the result for a row is kept while its elements and the column it reads are the same. NOT EXISTS, EXISTS inside an aggregate FILTER and expressions that can raise keep the normal plan.
query: @jsonb/items/elem_mapped_category

query/feature: IN, EXISTS, NOT EXISTS over a tree of joined tables (an inner join; a LEFT JOIN whose result gives the keys, behind a table of its own)
condition: the keys come from one table of the tree; PostgreSQL planned the tree as a join of its own, uncorrelated, serial and without a volatile function, and its keys fit half of work_mem
example: SELECT status, count(*) FROM orders WHERE tenant_id IN (SELECT s.id FROM tenants s JOIN dim_country c ON c.country_code = s.country_code WHERE c.continent <> 'north') GROUP BY status
notes: The plan PostgreSQL made of the tree runs once when the scan starts and gives the key set (duplicates and NULL keys as in the normal plan, an empty set matches no row, an anti join keeps a NULL key); a condition of the ON clause on the tree's own columns is already in that plan. A key of an expression over two tables of the tree (`IN (SELECT coalesce(a.k, b.k) FROM a LEFT JOIN b ..)` straight under the scan) is not pushed down: behind a table of its own (`t.id IN (SELECT coalesce(..) ..)`) it is.
query: @join/semi_tree

query/feature: LEFT JOIN LATERAL over jsonb_to_recordset or jsonb_array_elements of a list of the row, ON true or with conditions of its own
condition: a list of the scanned row (one level); a WHERE above the join that PostgreSQL could not make an inner join (it sees the NULL tuple), a lateral condition that may raise, or sift.agg_left_lateral off keeps the normal plan
example: SELECT o.id, max(o.total), avg(i.price) FROM orders o LEFT JOIN LATERAL jsonb_to_recordset(o.items) AS i(category text, price float8) ON true GROUP BY o.id
notes: A row none of whose elements passes (no list, an empty one, all failing the lateral's own conditions) is one tuple with NULL element columns, so a per-row group keeps its row; a row the snapshot does not see is no tuple.
query: @join/left_lateral

query/feature: FROM x, LATERAL (SELECT aggregates FROM f WHERE f.k = x.k) and JOIN LATERAL (..) ON true: the table grouped once by the tie column, joined to x
condition: kept only when the planner costs it below the lookups of the normal plan; a sub-select that reads the columns of another lateral sub-select keeps the normal plan
example: SELECT o.id, s.t FROM owners o, LATERAL (SELECT sum(i.amt) t FROM items i WHERE i.set_id = o.k) s
notes: An outer row whose key has no row gets NULL (0 for a count), a NULL key has none, a repeated outer row gets its group each time: the rows of the normal plan. 6000 outer rows over 200,000: 141-176 ms of lookups against 5.4-5.8 ms.

query/feature: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT g, aggregates FROM f WHERE f.k = x.k GROUP BY g [HAVING ..]) ON true (also JOIN and the comma form)
condition: kept only when the planner costs the grouped table below the lookups of the normal plan
example: SELECT o.id, s.cat, s.t FROM owners o LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT i.cat, sum(i.amt) t FROM items i WHERE i.set_id = o.k GROUP BY i.cat) s ON true
notes: f is grouped by k and g and joined to x by k; an outer row with no group is one row with NULLs under LEFT JOIN and no row under JOIN, as in the normal plan.
